In brief

Parody. "The muchtreasured and intricately embroidered ancient Irish facecloth […] rendered more beautiful still by the waters of sorrow which have passed over them and by the rich incrustations of time": after the Citizen expresses his contempt for Bloom's claim to be Irish by spitting a wad of phlegm onto the floor, and then wiping himself with his handkerchief, several lush sentences describe the humble cloth as a stunningly beautiful tapestry woven by ancient Irish artists. As in the account of a dog who speaks ancient Irish verse, this parody reprises the stylistic imitation of contemporary newspapers. As in the list of ancient Irish heroes carved on seastones, it features gigantically capacious lists, recalling the work of medieval scribes who decorated their manuscripts with copious, intricate ornamentation.

At more length

The best joke in this paragraph comes at the end, as the Citizen's tears are stylistically transformed into beautifying "waters of sorrow" and his dried snot into "the rich incrustrations of time." Equally enjoyable, though, is the way gigantism crams an impossible number of images onto a tiny square of cloth: the four evangelists presenting their four iconographic symbols to the four masters, a generous sampling of the ancient stone ruins that lie all over the Irish countryside, and a seemingly endless parade of other Irish natural and artificial wonders, bathetically undercut by inclusion of mundane modern places that no one would think to venerate. Readers are invited to suppose that this wealth of visual illustrations is similar to illuminated medieval manuscripts—ambitious labors of preserving traditional culture. 

The work in the handkerchief has been "attributed to Solomon of Droma and Manus Tomaltach og MacDonogh, authors of the Book of Ballymote." The Book of Ballymote is a manuscript produced around 1390-91 in the County Sligo, in the castle of Ballymote owned by a man named Tolmatoch mac Tadg or Tolmatoch mac Donogh (MacDonagh). Joyce mentions him and one of three scribes who produced the work, Solam (Solomon) Ó Droma. A second scribe was named Magnus (Manus) Ó Duigenan; his given name makes it into the list attached to MacDonagh's. The third scribe, not mentioned, was Robertus (Robert) Mac Sithigh (McSheehy). The book that these three men made was a compilation of earlier written works that MacDonagh must have owned, including some biblical and post-biblical history, much Irish history (the Lebor Gabála or Book of Invasions, and lives of Finn MacCool, Cormac, Patrick, and Brian Boru), smidgens of Homeric history, and discussions of Ogham script and the writing of poetry.

Medieval scribes in Ireland enriched their manuscripts with a wealth of intricate colored illustrations. The parody calls the three men "the Sligo illuminators" and catalogues the designs that they have managed to work into their other great artistic achievement: the Citizen's handkerchief. The corners of this piece of cloth hold images of "the four evangelists in turn presenting to each of the four masters his evangelical symbol, a bogoak sceptre, a North American puma (a far nobler king of beasts than the British article, be it said in passing), a Kerry calf and a golden eagle from Carrantuohill." Some medieval manuscripts, including the famous Book of Kells, depicted Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John iconographically as the four beasts that surround the throne of God in Revelation 4:7: "And the first beast was like a lion, and the second beast like a calf, and the third beast had a face as a man, and the fourth beast was like a flying eagle." Here these four gospel writers meet the Four Masters of Irish history (anachronistically, since they wrote their Annals in the early 17th century and the Ballymote scribes worked at the end of the 14th). The sceptre that Matthew carries in most illustrations is now made of good Irish bogoak, Mark's lion (an animal associated with the British empire) has been replaced by the more Hibernophilic American puma, Luke's calf seems destined to produce good Kerry butter, and John's eagle perches atop Carrantuohill, Ireland's highest mountain.

Hibernophilia also pervades "the emunctory field" (from Latin emungere = to wipe one's nose, also applied to other excretory functions). This field, no doubt snotgreen, shows "our ancient duns and raths and cromlechs and grianauns." Duns (Irish dún) and raths (Irish ráth) are names for the ancient stone or earthen ring-forts whose remains can be seen throughout the island. Cromlechs, more commonly known as dolmens, are megalithic portal tombs in which immense flat stones are perched horizontally atop three or more upright stones. Gifford, and also Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner, identify the grianán as a kind of sunroom in a castle, but the Grianán of Aileach (or Ailich) in County Donegal gives reason to think that the word may be roughly synonymous with "dun" and "rath."  This structure, rebuilt in the 19th century to recapture the 6th or 7th century glory of its Uí Néill builders, is a large round stone fort.

Also displayed on the emunctory field are various "seats of learning," no doubt a reference to the many monastic settlements that made early medieval Ireland, "island of saints and sages," famous as a powerhouse of religious scholarship. The last item in this list, "maledictive stones," could refer to several different kinds of ancient Celtic occult practice. Gifford says that heaps of round stones were "piled (and added to) as the monument to a disaster." Slote and his collaborators quote lines from Samuel Ferguson's Lays of the Western Gael suggesting that people rearranged the stones in these cairns to bring about blessings or curses. Still another possibility is that "malective stones" refers to bulláns. These neolithic "cursing stones" had bowl-shaped hollows into which a human hand could be inserted. Stirring pebbles inside the hole in an anti-clockwise direction effected a curse.

The parody's account of what is depicted on the handkerchief concludes with a swollen list of Irish natural wonders and ancient human constructions. As in the list of heroes carved on stones hanging from the belt of the "sinewyarmed hero," which includes the non-Irish Goliath, Confucius, Dante, Columbus, Napoleon, and so forth, this one sometimes dips bathetically into modern sites that have nothing to do with ancient Irish glories: "Sir Patrick Dun's hospital" on Grand Canal Street, perhaps included because his Scottish name accidentally echoes those dún ring-forts; the "Rathdown Union Workhouse at Loughlinstown," a poorhouse eight miles south of town that similarly recalls the word ráth; "the Scotch house," a Dublin pub; "the brewery of Messrs Arthur Guinness, Son and Company (Limited)," an impressively large but very drab Dublin landmark; “Jury's Hotel” on College Green; and “the Henry Street Warehouse,” a haberdasher's shop on fashionable Henry Street.

The list's natural wonders include "the bog of Allen," a large midlands bog regarded in Joyce's time not as an ecological treasure but a pestilential "bogswamp." Earlier in Cyclops the Citizen has decried Ireland's "millions of acres of marsh and bog to make us all die of consumption." Another geographical site of dubious merit is "Curley's hole," a very dangerous ocean bathing spot marked with warning signs just north of Dublin in Dollymount. In his verse broadside Gas from a Burner Joyce has the printer who burned every copy of Dubliners erupt in sarcastic frustration about the writer's fondness for naming specific Irish places: "Talk about Irish Names of Places! / It's a wonder to me, upon my soul, / He forgot to mention Curly's Hole." "Fingal's cave" is not even Irish, but one of seven caves on an uninhabited island in the Scottish Inner Hebrides. As Slote and his collaborators observe, it may have jumped into the list because Fingal was "an alternative name for Finn MacCool, which was used by the Scottish poet James Macpherson."

The growing tone of sarcasm extends into political invective. Giifford calls the "Tullamore jail” in County Offaly "as undistinguished a building as the town itself" and quotes an Irish popular rhyme: "Great Bog of Allen, swallow down / That odious heap call'd Philipstown; / And if thy maw can swallow more, / Pray take—and welcome—Tullamore." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner add that after the jail's opening in 1830, "various Irish nationalist campaigners endured imprisonment there; it was notorious for 'brutal and unjustifiable treatment'." The “Maynooth college refectory" appears in the list because, as Joe Hynes has observed several paragraphs earlier, when King Edward visited Ireland in 1903 the dining hall of Ireland's leading seminary was sycophantically adorned with his racing banners and pictures of his favorite horses. The handkerchief also displays "the three birthplaces of the first duke of Wellington.” Sources did differ on the birthplace of Arthur Wellesley, one of Great Britain's great military leaders, but none of them belong in a tribute to Irish nationalistic pride, and including pictures of three mutually contradictory possibilities is absurd.

With this paragraph the many imitations of ancient Irish glory as conceived by the Literary Revival come to an end. Seven more mocking parodies remain, several quite memorable, but Joyce appears to have decided to spare his reader any more plunges into the distant past.

John Hunt 2026
